mainTopic: Who is believed that a captive woman stayed pure: מה לי לשקר, her maidservant, 'תרתי לא עבדי', casual speech, and the case of רבי זכריה בן הקצב.
overview: This amud deals with who is believed when a woman who was taken captive says she stayed pure. First the גמרא finishes asking whether מה לי לשקר helps her. It compares her to רבא's case of the rented donkey, where אביי said the rule cannot beat known facts. The גמרא answers that her defilement is only a worry, not a known fact, so מה לי לשקר works for her. Next, the גמרא asks whether even her own maidservant is believed, since a משנה in גיטין says her own maidservant does not count. רב פפי, רב פפא and רב אשי each answer differently. רב אשי's answer rests on the rule 'תרתי לא עבדי': a person may hide the truth but will not also lie, and a story about רב חסדא and a violent man supports this rule. The גמרא then tests whether these views match a dispute between two ברייתות. It shows that רב פפא can explain the lenient ברייתא as casual speech (מסיח לפי תומו). A new משנה tells of רבי זכריה בן הקצב, whose testimony about his own wife was rejected, and how he kept her in a separate house anyway. The amud ends with אביי asking whether a divorcée may be housed the same way, and a ברייתא is brought to answer him.

steps.title: Do we say 'why would I lie' for the captive woman?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its question: do we believe the woman because of מה לי לשקר, or not?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we say 'why would I lie?' Or perhaps we do not say it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question. The woman could have made a stronger claim, so do we believe the weaker claim she actually made?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea behind מה לי לשקר is that if someone wanted to lie, they would have told a better lie. Since she chose a weaker claim, she is probably telling the truth. The question is whether this reasoning works in her case.

keyTerms.meaning: "Why would I lie?" We believe someone because they could have made a better claim and did not.

phrases.english: Why would I lie?
Or perhaps we do not say this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the question that began before this text.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the reasoning of מה לי לשקר makes the woman's claim of purity believable.

steps.title: Comparing her to the case of the rented donkey
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how her case is different from a well-known case of a rented donkey. It starts telling that story.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from that incident? A man rented his donkey to his friend and told him: Don't take the road by the Pekod River, where there is water. Take the Neresh road, where there is no water. The renter took the Pekod River road, and the donkey died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge. It begins telling a story that it will compare to the woman's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording 'how is this different' hints that the earlier case should decide our question. The facts matter here: everyone knows the Pekod road has water. That detail will become the key point.

keyTerms.meaning: And how is it different? (a challenge comparing two cases)

phrases.english: And how is this different from that incident,

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאֹגַר לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: where a certain man rented a donkey to his friend,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא תֵּיזִיל בְּאוֹרְחָא דִּנְהַר פְּקוֹד
phrases.english: and said to him: Do not go on the road of the Pekod River,
where there is water;
go on the road of Neresh, where there is no water.
And he went on the road of the Pekod River
and the donkey died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an earlier case that seems to answer the question in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that מה לי לשקר should help the captive woman.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the donkey case, the rule was rejected because it went against known facts. The woman's case may be similar.

steps.title: רבא believes the renter: 'Why would I lie?'
steps.stepSummary: The renter admits he took the forbidden road but says there was no water. רבא believes him because he could have claimed he took the safe road.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רבא and said: Yes, I took the Pekod River road, but there was no water. רבא said: 'Why would I lie?' If he wanted to, he could have said, I took the Neresh road.
steps.whatsHappening: The story goes on. רבא uses מה לי לשקר to believe the renter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renter could have lied completely and said he took the safe road. Instead he admitted the risky road and only denied that there was water. רבא reasons that someone who admits that much is probably honest about the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: Before him (coming to a judge for a ruling)

phrases.english: He came before Rava,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִין, בְּאוֹרְחָא דִּנְהַר פְּקוֹד אֲזַלִי,
phrases.english: and said to him: Yes, I went on the road of the Pekod River,
but there was no water.
phrases.notes: He means the water did not kill the donkey, so he should not have to pay.

phrases.english: Rava said: 'Why would I lie?'
If he wanted, he could have said to him:
I went on the road of Neresh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבא's ruling in the donkey story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא believes the renter that there was no water, because he could have made a better claim (that he took the safe road).

steps.title: אביי: the rule does not work against witnesses
steps.stepSummary: אביי says מה לי לשקר does not work when it goes against what witnesses know. Everyone knows there is water on that road.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: We do not say 'why would I lie' where there are witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי rejects רבא's reasoning. This finishes the גמרא's challenge to the captive woman's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מה לי לשקר can support a claim, but it cannot beat known facts. It is common knowledge that the Pekod road has water, so the renter's claim fails. The challenge is that the woman's claim should fail the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Where there are witnesses (where the facts are already known)

steps.confusionAlert: There were no actual witnesses in court here. 'Witnesses' means the fact is so well known that it counts as if witnesses had testified.

phrases.english: And Abaye said to him:

phrases.aramaic: ״מָה לִי לְשַׁקֵּר״ בִּמְקוֹם עֵדִים לָא אָמְרִינַן.
phrases.english: 'Why would I lie' is not said in a place of witnesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לִי לְשַׁקֵּר בִּמְקוֹם עֵדִים לָא אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבא's ruling in step 3. This is the point of the challenge from step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבא's use of מה לי לשקר in the donkey case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The claim goes against facts everyone knows, and מה לי לשקר cannot beat known facts.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a limit on מה לי לשקר: it works only when it does not go against established facts.

steps.title: A sure fact versus a mere worry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the cases are different. With the donkey, it is certain that the road has water. With the woman, it is only a worry that she was defiled, so מה לי לשקר still works.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them? There, there are surely witnesses that there is water. Here, was she definitely defiled? It is only a worry, and where there is only a worry, we do say it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the comparison. It shows the woman's case is different, so we can believe her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's limit applies only when a fact is certain. We do not know that a captive woman was defiled; we only worry that she might have been. A mere worry is not like witnesses, so her מה לי לשקר works.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? (pushing away a comparison)
A worry or concern, not a known fact

steps.whatToRemember: מה לי לשקר cannot beat a certain fact (like witnesses), but it can beat a mere worry. So the captive woman who says she stayed pure is believed.

phrases.english: How can you compare?!

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם וַדַּאי אִיכָּא עֵדִים דְּאִיכָּא מַיָּא.
phrases.english: There, there are certainly witnesses that there is water.
Here, was she definitely defiled?
It is only a worry,
and where there is only a worry, we do say it.
phrases.notes: 'It' means the rule of 'why would I lie', so her claim is accepted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 2 to 4 by showing the cases are different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: a certain fact versus a doubtful worry.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The woman's case is like the donkey case, so מה לי לשקר should not help her.
steps.terutzMaskana: Her defilement is only a worry, not a known fact, so מה לי לשקר works and she is believed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: מה לי לשקר works against a mere worry, but not against something witnesses or common knowledge make certain.

steps.title: The משנה: Even a Slave or Maidservant Is Believed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה: if there are witnesses that the captive woman was not defiled, even a slave or a maidservant is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there are witnesses, even a slave and even a maidservant are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה so it can ask a question about it. This step sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a slave or maidservant cannot serve as a valid witness. The משנה is lenient here and lets them testify that a captive woman stayed pure. The גמרא will now ask how far this leniency goes.

phrases.english: If there are witnesses,
phrases.notes: This is quoted from our משנה about women in a captured city. The witnesses would say she was not defiled.

phrases.english: even a slave and even a maidservant are believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם יֵשׁ עֵדִים, אֲפִילּוּ עֶבֶד וַאֲפִילּוּ שִׁפְחָה נֶאֱמָנִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה after the מה לי לשקר discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a captive woman, even a slave or maidservant is believed to testify that she was not defiled.

steps.title: Contradiction: Her Own Maidservant Doesn't Count in the Divorce Case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether even her own maidservant is believed. A משנה about a conditional divorce says her own maidservant is not enough of a guard, because she feels too comfortable around her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is even her own maidservant believed? But a משנה says: She may be alone with him only in the presence of witnesses, even a slave or a maidservant, except for her own maidservant, because she is at ease with her own maidservant!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether our משנה includes the woman's own personal maidservant. It then brings a different משנה that seems to say her own maidservant does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the גיטין case, a witness must be present so the couple will not be together. A woman is not embarrassed in front of her own maidservant, so that maidservant does not stop anything. If her own maidservant does not count there, why should she be believed here about a captive?

keyTerms.meaning: and contrast it with (a source that seems to contradict)
she will be alone (in יחוד) with him

steps.confusionAlert: The גיטין case is about a man who divorced his wife on a condition. Being alone together before the condition is met causes a problem. It is not about captives at all. The גמרא is only comparing how each case treats her own maidservant.

phrases.english: And is even her own maidservant believed?
And contrast it with this:
phrases.notes: The source is a משנה in גיטין 73a, about a man who divorced his wife on a condition.

phrases.english: She may not be alone with him
except in the presence of witnesses.
And even in the presence of a slave
and in the presence of a maidservant,
except for her own maidservant,
because she is at ease with her own maidservant!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the leniency in step 6 reaches.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a maidservant is believed for a captive woman.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The גיטין משנה says her own maidservant is not a reliable guard. So her own maidservant should not be trusted for a captive either.

steps.title: רב פפי: The Rabbis Were Lenient for a Captive
steps.stepSummary: רב פפי answers that for a שבויה the rabbis were extra lenient, so even her own maidservant is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפי said: With a captive woman, they were lenient.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפי answers the contradiction by saying the captive case is special. There the rabbis went easy, even with her own maidservant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry that a captive was defiled is only a concern, not a known fact. So the rabbis accepted weaker testimony there, even from her own maidservant. In the divorce case they did not relax the rule.
steps.confusionAlert: רב פפי (this step) and רב פפא (next step) are two different rabbis with similar names, and they give two different answers.

phrases.english: Rav Pappi said:
With a captive woman, they were lenient.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: a special leniency for a captive.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Her own maidservant should be equally untrustworthy in both cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: For a captive, the rabbis were lenient and accept even her own maidservant.

steps.title: רב פפא: Our משנה Means the Husband's Maidservant
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers differently. The divorce case is about her own maidservant, who is not trusted. Our משנה is about his maidservant, who is trusted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: This one is about her maidservant, and that one is about his maidservant.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a second answer. He says the two משניות are talking about different maidservants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב פפא, her own maidservant is never good enough, even for a captive. Our משנה only trusts a maidservant who belongs to the husband, because the woman is not as close to her. This way there is no contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: this one... that one (each source deals with a different case)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
This one is about her maidservant,
phrases.notes: 'This one' means the divorce case in גיטין. There her own maidservant is not trusted.

phrases.english: that one is about his maidservant.
phrases.notes: 'That one' means our משנה about the captive. It is talking about the husband's maidservant.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: הָא בְּשִׁפְחָה דִּידַהּ, הָא בְּשִׁפְחָה דִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the contradiction in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the two sources discuss different maidservants.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה includes her own maidservant.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה only means the husband's maidservant; her own is never trusted.

steps.title: Challenge to רב פפא: 'A Person Can't Testify About Himself'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא. The משנה says a person cannot testify about himself, which implies that her own maidservant can.
steps.simpleTranslation: And her own maidservant is not believed? But the משנה teaches: A person cannot testify about himself. That implies her own maidservant is believed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב פפא's answer using a line from our משנה. It reads that line as if her own maidservant is believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only excludes the woman herself. By saying only 'himself', it seems to allow everyone else, including her own maidservant. That goes against רב פפא, who said her own maidservant is never trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: a person cannot testify about himself

phrases.english: And her own maidservant is not believed?
But it teaches:
A person cannot testify about himself,
phrases.notes: This line is in our משנה. It means the woman cannot testify that she herself stayed pure.

phrases.english: which implies her own maidservant is believed!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשִׁפְחָה דִּידַהּ לָא מְהֵימְנָא? הָא קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's answer from step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that her own maidservant is never believed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה only excludes the woman herself, so it seems everyone else, even her own maidservant, is believed.

steps.title: Her Maidservant Counts as Herself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that her own maidservant is treated just like the woman herself. So 'himself' includes her maidservant too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Her maidservant is also considered like herself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב פפא. It says the word 'himself' in the משנה also covers her own maidservant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her own maidservant is so close to her that the law treats her like the woman herself. So when the משנה says a person cannot testify about himself, her maidservant is included. רב פפא's answer stands.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers. רב פפי: for a captive the rabbis were lenient, so even her own maidservant is believed. רב פפא: only the husband's maidservant is believed. Her own maidservant counts like the woman herself, and she cannot testify about herself.

phrases.english: Her maidservant also
is considered like herself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 and saves רב פפא's position.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the משנה's word 'himself' more broadly.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Himself' means only the woman, so her maidservant is believed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Her own maidservant is treated like her, so she is also not believed.

steps.title: Silence versus speaking: when the maidservant is believed
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says both sources are about her own maidservant. The difference is whether her silence would help or hurt the woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Both cases are about her own maidservant. A maidservant may see something and keep quiet. In the divorce case, her silence is enough to permit the woman, so she is not believed. In the שבויה case, her silence would forbid the woman, so she is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a new, third answer to the contradiction from Step 7. He says the deciding factor is what her silence would do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike רב פפא, רב אשי says both cases really are about her own maidservant. A loyal maidservant might hide the truth by keeping quiet. In the divorce case, all she has to say is 'I was there', and keeping quiet about anything that happened permits the woman. In the שבויה case, the woman is assumed forbidden, so silence does not help her. The maidservant would have to actively speak up and say 'she was not defiled'.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. In the divorce case, the maidservant's silence HELPS the wife, so we don't trust her. In the שבויה case, her silence would HURT the wife, so when she speaks up we trust her.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Both this and that are about her own maidservant,
phrases.notes: 'This and that' means the divorce case from Step 7 and our משנה about the captive woman.

phrases.english: and a maidservant does see and keep silent.
There, where her silence permits her, she is not believed.
Here, where her silence forbids her, she is believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: הָא וְהָא בְּשִׁפְחָה דִּידַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third resolution of the contradiction raised in Step 7, alongside רב פפי and רב פפא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by whether silence helps or hurts the woman
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A maidservant who is loyal to her mistress can never be trusted about her.
steps.terutzMaskana: She may hide the truth by staying quiet, but she is trusted when she has to actively speak in order to help.

steps.title: But maybe she will just lie
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even in the שבויה case, maybe the maidservant will lie to help her mistress.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even here, she can come and lie!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אשי. If the maidservant is loyal enough to keep quiet, why wouldn't she also lie for her mistress?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי's answer depends on the idea that silence is different from speaking. The challenge says that someone willing to hide the truth might also be willing to say something false.

phrases.english: Now too, she can come and lie!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of רב אשי in Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that the maidservant is believed when she speaks up in the שבויה case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone loyal enough to stay silent might also be loyal enough to lie, so her testimony should not be trusted.

steps.title: She will not do two wrongs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a person does not do two wrongs, keeping quiet and also lying.
steps.simpleTranslation: She does not do two things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Staying quiet is one wrong, and lying would be a second one. We assume she will not do both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hiding the truth is a smaller step than saying something false. We suspect her of the smaller wrong, but not of adding an active lie on top of it.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule 'תרתי לא עבדי': a person may hide the truth, but we do not suspect him of also actively lying.

phrases.english: She does not do two things.
phrases.notes: The 'two things' are staying quiet about the truth and also saying something false.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Introducing a general principle about human behavior
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Someone who stays quiet to help might also lie.
steps.terutzMaskana: People do not do two wrongs. Hiding the truth does not mean someone will lie.

steps.title: A man claims to be a long-lost brother
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a story to support the idea of 'two wrongs'. A man comes to מרי בר איסק claiming to be his brother and asks for part of the inheritance.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like the case of מרי בר איסק (some say חנא בר איסק). A brother came to him from בי חוזאה and said: Give me my share of our father's property! He answered: I don't know you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a story that will show the same principle. Here we only hear the background: a stranger claims to be a brother, and the man says he doesn't know him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man came from a faraway place, so it is believable that the brother would not recognize him. The story will end with the same line, 'תרתי לא עבדי', which is why it is brought here.

keyTerms.meaning: divide for me, give me my share

phrases.english: Like that case of Mari bar Isak,
and some say it was Chana bar Isak,
a brother came to him from Bei Chozaa.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: פְּלוֹג לִי בְּנִכְסֵי דְּאַבָּא!
phrases.english: He said to him: Give me my share of our father's property!
He said to him: I don't know you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that supports the principle from Step 14.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that a person does not do two wrongs (stay silent and also lie)
steps.raayaSupportSource: A real court case judged by רב חסדא

steps.title: רב חסדא says the brother may really not recognize him
steps.stepSummary: The man goes to רב חסדא, who says מרי's answer makes sense. A beard can change how someone looks, as with יוסף and his brothers.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רב חסדא. רב חסדא said: He is right, as it says, 'And יוסף recognized his brothers but they did not recognize him.' This teaches that יוסף left without a beard and came back with a beard.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא first agrees that it is reasonable for מרי not to recognize his brother. He brings a proof from the story of יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מרי's 'I don't know you' is not automatically a lie. A person who left young may look very different years later, just as יוסף's brothers did not recognize him once he had grown a beard.

keyTerms.meaning: he is speaking correctly to you
the first full growth of a beard

phrases.english: He came before Rav Chisda.
He said to him: He is speaking correctly to you,
phrases.notes: רב חסדא is telling the claimant that מרי's answer, 'I don't know you', makes sense.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'And Joseph recognized his brothers,'
'but they did not recognize him,'
this teaches that he left without a full beard
and came back with a full beard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story. רב חסדא first agrees that מרי's claim is reasonable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is believable that a brother would not recognize someone who left long ago, so 'I don't know you' is a fair answer.

steps.title: רב חסדא makes the strong man bring witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא tells the claimant to bring witnesses. He says the witnesses are afraid of מרי, who is violent, so רב חסדא tells מרי to bring witnesses that this is not his brother.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Go bring witnesses that you are his brother. He said: I have witnesses, but they are afraid of him, because he is a violent man. So רב חסדא said to מרי: You go bring witnesses that he is not your brother.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא first follows the normal rule and asks the claimant for witnesses. When he hears that the witnesses are scared, he flips the burden onto מרי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the person making the claim has to prove it. Here the witnesses won't come forward because they fear מרי. So רב חסדא makes מרי produce witnesses instead: for his witnesses to help him, they would have to say something false. The גמרא will soon ask whether they might do that (Step 20).

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: זִיל אַיְיתִי סָהֲדֵי דַּאֲחוּהּ אַתְּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: Go bring witnesses that you are his brother.
He said to him: I have witnesses,
but they are afraid of him, because he is a violent man.
He said to the other one himself:
phrases.notes: Now רב חסדא turns to מרי, the man being asked to share the property.

phrases.aramaic: זִיל אַיְיתִינְהוּ אַתְּ דְּלָאו אֲחוּךְ הוּא.
phrases.english: You go bring them, that he is not your brother.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: זִיל אַיְיתִי סָהֲדֵי דַּאֲחוּהּ אַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story with רב חסדא's actual ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the claimant's witnesses are scared of a violent defendant, the defendant must bring witnesses to support his side.

steps.title: מרי protests: the claimant should bring proof
steps.stepSummary: מרי objects that the usual rule puts the burden of proof on the person making the claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: מרי said: Is this the law? The one who wants to take money from his friend must bring the proof!
steps.whatsHappening: מרי challenges רב חסדא's ruling, quoting a well-known rule of the courts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic rule is that whoever wants to take something from another person must prove his claim. מרי argues that the claimant should have to prove he is a brother, not that מרי should have to prove he isn't.

keyTerms.meaning: the one who wants to take from another must bring the proof

phrases.english: He said to him: Is this the law?
The one who takes from his fellow must bring the proof!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: מרי challenges רב חסדא's ruling from Step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's ruling that מרי must bring witnesses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The standard rule puts the burden of proof on the claimant, not on the person holding the property.

steps.title: This is how violent men are judged
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers that this is the way he judges מרי and all violent people like him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: This is how I judge you and all your violent friends.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא defends his ruling. For violent people, whom others are afraid to testify against, the burden is put on them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual rule assumes witnesses can speak freely. When a person scares off the witnesses, the court makes that person bring the proof instead.

phrases.english: He said to him: This is how I judge you
and all your violent friends.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מרי's objection in Step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The burden of proof always falls on the claimant.
steps.terutzMaskana: When the defendant is a violent man, the court puts the burden on him.

steps.title: But his witnesses will just lie
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what this ruling achieves. Witnesses afraid of מרי could simply come and lie for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: But now too, they can come and lie!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רב חסדא's ruling. If the witnesses fear מרי, they could falsely say the man is not his brother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If fear keeps the witnesses quiet, maybe fear will also push them to lie in מרי's favor. Then making מרי bring witnesses would not help at all.

phrases.english: Now too, they can come and lie!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same kind of question as Step 13, now asked about the witnesses in the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: The usefulness of רב חסדא's ruling
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Scared witnesses might lie for the violent man, so his witnesses prove nothing.

steps.title: Witnesses will not do two wrongs
steps.stepSummary: The answer is the same principle: the witnesses may stay quiet out of fear, but they will not also lie.
steps.simpleTranslation: They do not do two things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the story with the same answer as Step 14. This shows that רב חסדא relied on the principle that people do not do two wrongs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fear can make witnesses avoid testifying, which is one wrong. Lying in court would be a second, bigger wrong, and we do not suspect them of it. This supports רב אשי's claim that the maidservant may stay quiet but will not lie.
steps.whatToRemember: Both the maidservant and the scared witnesses follow one principle: 'תרתי לא עבדי'. Someone may hide the truth by staying silent, but we do not suspect him of also lying. This is why the maidservant is believed for a שבויה.
steps.whyThisMatters: The story shows that 'תרתי לא עבדי' is a real rule that courts used, not just an idea made up to answer one question.

phrases.english: They do not do two things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 20 and completes the proof for Step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A person may stay silent to avoid trouble or to help someone, but is not suspected of also lying. This supports רב אשי's answer about the maidservant.

steps.title: Is the maidservant argument the same as an argument between two ברייתות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that the אמוראים' dispute about the maidservant matches two ברייתות that disagree about who may testify for a captive woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is like a dispute between תנאים. One ברייתא says that a man, a woman, a boy, a girl, her father, mother, brother and sister may testify that she was not defiled, but not her son, daughter, slave or maidservant. Another ברייתא says everyone is believed except the woman herself and her husband.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wonders whether the argument about the maidservant is really an older argument found in two ברייתות. It quotes both ברייתות to set up the comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא clearly says her maidservant (שפחתה) is NOT believed. The second ברייתא says everyone except her and her husband IS believed, which seems to include her maidservant. So the two ברייתות appear to disagree on exactly the question the אמוראים argued about.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this matches a dispute between תנאים?

steps.confusionAlert: Both ברייתות are about testimony that a captive woman was NOT defiled, so she may still marry a כהן. They are not about ordinary court cases.

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute of Tannaim:
This testimony —
phrases.notes: He means testimony that a captive woman was not defiled while in captivity.

phrases.english: a man and a woman, a boy and a girl,
her father and her mother, and her brother and her sister [are believed].
but not her son and her daughter,
not her slave and her maidservant.
And it is taught in another baraita:
All are believed to testify,
except for her and her husband.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story of מרי ends, the גמרא goes back to the earlier dispute about the maidservant and looks for it among the תנאים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the אמוראים' dispute about the maidservant match the disagreement between these two ברייתות?

steps.title: רב פפי and רב אשי depend on the ברייתות, but what about רב פפא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא grants that רב פפי and רב אשי follow one side of the תנאים' dispute, and asks whether רב פפא's view must also depend on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The view of רב פפי and רב אשי is certainly a dispute of תנאים. But must we say that the view of רב פפא is a dispute of תנאים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sorts the אמוראים: those who believe her maidservant clearly agree with the second ברייתא and disagree with the first. It then asks whether רב פפא, who does not believe her maidservant, is also stuck on one side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפי and רב אשי hold that her maidservant is believed, which openly contradicts the first ברייתא. רב פפא holds that her maidservant is not believed. The question is whether he must reject the second ברייתא, or whether he can explain it so that it fits his view.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute of תנאים

phrases.english: The opinion of Rav Pappi and of Rav Ashi
is a dispute of Tannaim.
The opinion of Rav Pappa — must we
phrases.notes: Some versions add the word in square brackets, and that word turns this line into a question.

phrases.english: say it is a dispute of Tannaim?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַב פַּפֵּי וּדְרַב אָשֵׁי תַּנָּאֵי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the proposal of Step 22, accepting it for two אמוראים and questioning it for רב פפא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can רב פפא's view fit both ברייתות, or must he side with only one?

steps.title: רב פפא explains the lenient ברייתא as casual speech
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא can say the second ברייתא speaks about someone who talks casually, not someone giving formal testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא could say to you: when that ברייתא was taught, it was about a case where she was speaking casually, without meaning to testify.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how רב פפא can avoid taking sides. He reads the second ברייתא as talking about casual remarks (מסיח לפי תומו).
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a person mentions a fact in passing, while talking about something else, it is more trustworthy than deliberate testimony. So the second ברייתא, which believes everyone, means only casual remarks. Formal testimony from her maidservant is still not accepted, just as the first ברייתא says.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you, meaning this is how he would answer
Speaking innocently and in passing, without intending to testify

steps.whyThisMatters: This introduces the important idea of מסיח לפי תומו: casual, unplanned speech can be trusted even from people who could not testify formally.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa could say to you:
When that baraita was taught,
it was in a case where she speaks innocently, without intent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 23 by limiting the second ברייתא to casual speech.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the lenient ברייתא is about casual speech only.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב פפא must reject the ברייתא that believes everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both ברייתות fit רב פפא: formal testimony from her maidservant is rejected, but casual remarks are accepted.

steps.title: A son's casual remarks let his mother marry a כהן
steps.stepSummary: A story shows that casual remarks are accepted even from someone who could not testify formally. A son's offhand words about his captive mother were trusted.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what רב דימי reported when he came. רב חנן of Carthage told of a case before רבי יהושע בן לוי, and some say רבי יהושע בן לוי told of a case before רבי. A man was talking casually and said: 'My mother and I were taken captive among the gentiles. When I went to draw water, my mind was on my mother. When I went to gather wood, my mind was on my mother.' And רבי let her marry into כהונה based on his words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story to back up the idea of casual speech from Step 24. A son, who normally cannot testify for his mother, was believed because he spoke in passing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא said a son is NOT believed about his mother. Yet רבי relied on the son's words because he was not trying to testify; he was just telling his story. This shows that casual speech works even from someone who could not testify formally, so the same can be true of her maidservant.

keyTerms.meaning: My mind was on my mother, meaning I kept watch over her
Allowed her to marry a כהן

steps.whatToRemember: רב פפא's view fits both ברייתות. Her maidservant cannot formally testify for her, but casual remarks (מסיח לפי תומו) are believed even from relatives like a son. The story of רבי proves this.
steps.confusionAlert: The son was not called in as a witness. His words count precisely BECAUSE he was not trying to testify.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּכִי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר:
phrases.english: As in this case: when Rav Dimi came, he said:
Rav Chanan of Carthage relates:

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲשֶׂה בָּא לִפְנֵי רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי,
phrases.english: An incident came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי מִישְׁתַּעֵי:
phrases.english: and some say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi relates:
An incident came before Rabbi
phrases.notes: Plain "רבי" here means רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.aramaic: בְּאָדָם אֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה מֵסִיחַ לְפִי תּוּמּוֹ,
phrases.english: concerning a man who was speaking innocently, in passing,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: אֲנִי וְאִמִּי נִשְׁבִּינוּ לְבֵין הַגּוֹיִם.
phrases.english: and he said: My mother and I were taken captive among the gentiles.

phrases.aramaic: יָצָאתִי לִשְׁאוֹב מַיִם — דַּעְתִּי עַל אִמִּי,
phrases.english: When I went out to draw water — my mind was on my mother;
to gather wood — my mind was on my mother.
And Rabbi allowed her to marry into the priesthood based on his word.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּכִי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 24's idea that casual speech is accepted, even from someone who could not testify formally.
steps.raayaObject: That מסיח לפי תומו is believed even from someone who is not a valid witness for her.
steps.raayaSupportSource: An incident before רבי (or before רבי יהושע בן לוי) where a son's casual remarks let his captive mother marry a כהן.

steps.title: A husband swears his wife never left his side
steps.stepSummary: רבי זכריה בן הקצב swears that his wife's hand never left his own hand for the whole time the gentiles were in ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: רבי זכריה בן הקצב said: By this holy Temple! Her hand did not leave my hand from the moment the gentiles entered ירושלים until they left.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens with a real story. A husband tries to prove his wife was never violated during the conquest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the theme of a captive woman, who is suspected of having been violated. Being with gentile conquerors would forbid her to a husband who is a כהן, so רבי זכריה tries to clear her with his own word.

keyTerms.meaning: 'By this dwelling place!' An oath by the בית המקדש, the home of the שכינה
Her hand did not move away, meaning she was never out of my sight

phrases.english: MISHNA
Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav said:
By this abode!
phrases.notes: He is swearing by the בית המקדש, the place where the שכינה rests.

phrases.english: Her hand did not move from my hand
from the time that gentiles entered Jerusalem
until they left.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זְכַרְיָה בֶּן הַקַּצָּב: הַמָּעוֹן הַזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה that continues the general topic of captive women.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband testifies under oath that his wife was never left alone with the conquerors.

steps.title: The Sages reject his testimony
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer that a person cannot testify about himself, so his word does not permit his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: A person cannot testify about himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים turn down רבי זכריה's testimony.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A man's wife counts like himself for testimony, so testifying about her is testifying about himself. Even though he swore an oath, his testimony is not accepted and she stays forbidden to him.

keyTerms.meaning: A person does not testify about himself

steps.confusionAlert: The חכמים are not calling him a liar. The rule is that a person's testimony about himself, or about his wife, simply does not count as testimony.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why the wife stays forbidden. It sets up the ברייתא's story of how he lived with that ruling.

phrases.english: They said to him:
A person does not testify about himself.
phrases.notes: A man's wife is treated like himself here, so testifying for her is like testifying for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אֵין אָדָם מֵעִיד עַל עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the testimony given in step 26.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The husband's testimony about his own wife
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A person is not a valid witness about himself, and his wife counts as himself.

steps.title: How he kept his wife without being alone with her
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says he did not divorce her. He gave her a separate house in his courtyard and used their sons as a buffer so they were never alone together.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: And even so, he set aside a house for her in his courtyard. When she went out, she went out ahead of her sons, and when she came in, she came in after her sons.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that adds what happened after the ruling. He kept her close but made sure they were never alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה made her forbidden to him, but the ברייתא shows he did not divorce her. She went out ahead of her sons and came in after them, so she was never left alone with her husband in the courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גְּמָרָא, the discussion that follows the משנה
He set aside a house for her

phrases.english: GEMARA
It was taught: And even so,
phrases.notes: Even though the חכמים ruled she was forbidden to him.

phrases.english: he designated a house for her in his courtyard,
and when she goes out, she goes out ahead of her sons,
and when she enters, she enters after her sons.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא describing how the husband lived with the משנה's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A forbidden wife may live in a separate house in the husband's courtyard if safeguards keep them from being alone together.

steps.title: אביי asks if a divorcée can be housed the same way
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks whether the same arrangement is allowed for a divorced wife, or only for a captive, where the rule is more lenient.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked: May one do the same with a divorcée? Is it only there, because the חכמים were lenient with a captive woman, but here it is not allowed? Or perhaps there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי asks whether the courtyard arrangement from the ברייתא also works for a man and his divorced wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A captive is only suspected of being violated, so the חכמים were lenient with her. A divorcée is definitely forbidden to a כהן, so maybe the same arrangement is too risky. Or maybe the safeguard is equally good in both cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks, introducing a question the asker is unsure about
Or perhaps there is no difference

phrases.english: Abaye asked:
What is the law about doing likewise with a divorcée?
Is it only there, because with a captive woman they were lenient,
but here, not?
Or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי אַבָּיֵי: מַהוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת בִּגְרוּשָׁה כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks whether the ברייתא's leniency for a captive also applies to a divorcée.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a divorced wife may live in her former husband's courtyard with the same safeguards used for the captive wife.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a divorcée living near her ex-husband
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to answer אביי from a ברייתא that says a divorced woman may not marry and live in her ex-husband's neighborhood.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as it was taught: One who divorces his wife, she may not marry in his neighborhood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to answer אביי's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא keeps a divorcée from living close to her former husband, because their past closeness could lead to sin. If even living nearby is a problem, the courtyard arrangement might be forbidden for a divorcée. The גמרא will look at this source more closely next.

phrases.english: Come and hear, as it was taught:
One who divorces his wife,
she may not marry in his neighborhood.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּתַנְיָא: הַמְגָרֵשׁ אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to try to answer אביי's question from step 29.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a divorcée may live in her former husband's courtyard
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that forbids a divorcée to marry and live in her former husband's neighborhood
